meta.title: Our Lady of La Salette — Chronology
meta.subtitle: Chronology of the reported apparition at La Salette in its setting — the famine year, the shrine, the congregation and the Church's judgments (1826–2016)
meta.description: An open, source-referenced chronology of the Marian apparition reported at La Salette-Fallavaux in 1846: the famine year and the diocese it happened in, the cures reported afterwards, the diocesan approval of 1851, the basilica and the Missionaries of La Salette, and the later controversy over the "Secrets of La Salette".
meta.dataQualityNote: Work-in-progress dataset compiled from public sources (see references). The apparition is recorded here as a REPORTED event: the dataset states who reported what and when, and what the Church ruled and when, citing the ruling document — it never asserts the supernatural claim as fact. Events before 1846 (the subsistence crisis, the diocese of Grenoble under de Bruillard) are CONTEXT for the setting, offered neither as explanation of the report nor as corroboration of it. Reported cures are handled the same way: the datable thing is the ACCOUNT — that a cure was reported, by whom, when it began to circulate, and when the commission or Rousselot's printed report took it up. No cure is recorded as having happened; La Salette has no medical bureau and no cure connected with it carries an act of recognition. Attendance figures are attributed to whoever publishes them and are left unreconciled where they disagree. The two Church judgments this dataset carries are about two different objects — the apparition (approved 1851) and the expanded "secrets" (restricted 1915 and 1923) — and are never merged. Contested claims are attributed to their authors; dates not yet verified against a primary source are flagged with a ? mark. Corrections against primary sources are welcome.

facts.label: What it is
facts.value: A single Marian apparition reported on 19 September 1846 on a mountain above La Salette-Fallavaux (French Alps, then diocese of Grenoble) by two shepherd children — recorded here as the children's account and as the Church judgments passed on it, not as an asserted fact.

facts.label: The seers
facts.value: Mélanie Calvat, aged 14 (the 1910 Catholic Encyclopedia says 15), and Maximin Giraud, aged 11 — two shepherd children of Corps who reported a weeping "Beautiful Lady" and a message delivered partly in French, partly in the local Occitan dialect.

facts.label: Church approval status
facts.value: Two separate judgments about two separate objects. (1) The apparition: declared to bear "all the characteristics of truth" and worthy of belief by Bishop Philibert de Bruillard of Grenoble on 19 September 1851. (2) Mélanie's later, expanded "Secret": restricted by the Holy Office — a decree of 21 December 1915 ordered the faithful not to discuss the secret under its various forms, and a decree of 9 May 1923 placed the 1922 reprint of her 1879 booklet on the Index of Forbidden Books. The 1915 decree states expressly that devotion to Our Lady of La Salette itself is not forbidden.

facts.label: Institutions born of it
facts.value: The Sanctuary (later Basilica) of Our Lady of La Salette on the apparition site, and the Missionaries of Our Lady of La Salette, both announced by Bishop de Bruillard's pastoral letter of 1 May 1852.

facts.label: Reported cures
facts.value: Cures were claimed at the mountain from the autumn of 1846, and the reports — with the press controversy around them — are what brought Bishop de Bruillard to open the canonical inquiry in July 1847; the commission examined them, and Canon Rousselot printed the case for them in his report to the bishop. That is as far as this dataset goes: it records who reported what and when, and never that a cure occurred. La Salette has no medical bureau and no equivalent of the Lourdes recognition acts — the French Wikipedia article states plainly that the Church made no scientific inquiry into these "declarations of miracles" — so no cure connected with the shrine carries a dated act of recognition, and none is recorded here as a fact.

facts.label: Pilgrimage today
facts.value: Two figures circulate and they do not agree. Villes Sanctuaires en France, the association of French shrine towns of which La Salette is a member, gives nearly 200,000 pilgrims and visitors a year; the French Wikipedia article gives about 300,000. Neither states a method, and no audited count published by the sanctuary itself was reachable. Both numbers are attributed to whoever publishes them and the gap is left standing.

approvalLadder.note: Two things were judged here, by different authorities, about different objects, and this page never adds them up. The apparition reported on 19 September 1846 was investigated by the Bishop of Grenoble and declared worthy of belief on 19 September 1851; that judgment has never been revoked. Rome then acted fast and generously on the cult — nine acts between August and December 1852, from a privileged altar to an archconfraternity to the anniversary in the diocesan calendar — without ever ruling on whether the apparition happened, a gap the bishop who catalogued those favours in 1854 states in as many words. The Holy Office acts of 1915 and 1923 concern a third object again — the expanded "Secret" texts Mélanie Calvat wrote and published decades afterwards — and the 1915 decree states in so many words that devotion to Our Lady of La Salette is not thereby forbidden. No Roman doctrinal ruling on the 1846 apparition itself has been located, in either direction. Reading the 1852 favours as Rome's approval, or the 1915 and 1923 decrees as Rome's verdict against, are the two most common errors in the literature — sympathetic and critical alike, and they are the same error.

stages.label: Parish level — local inquiry
stages.who: The parish clergy of La Salette, in the diocese of Grenoble
stages.noDocument: No distinct parish-level canonical inquiry has been located. What the sources record at this level is pastoral rather than judicial: the children were urged to tell the parish priest of La Salette, who took notes and recounted their account in his sermon the next morning, and the English Wikipedia article states that on 16 October 1846 the parish priest wrote down where the two children's accounts differed. Searched for a parish-level process or finding in the sanctuary's own history, the 1910 Catholic Encyclopedia article and the English Wikipedia article: all three pass straight from the children's report to the bishop's commissions, and none names a local canonical inquiry or a ruling by one. That is a statement about the record, not a claim that nothing happened at La Salette before 1847.

stages.label: Diocese of Grenoble — the apparition
stages.who: Bishop Philibert de Bruillard, with commissions of clergy and theologians
stages.outcome: The bishop appointed a commission to examine the event judicially; the 1910 Catholic Encyclopedia records that it concluded the reality of the apparition should be admitted. After what the sanctuary describes as five years of rigorous investigation, de Bruillard's doctrinal pronouncement of 19 September 1851 declared that the apparition of the Blessed Virgin to the two shepherds bears within itself all the characteristics of truth and that the faithful have good grounds to hold it certain, and authorised the cult. This is the judgment on the apparition, it is diocesan, and it has never been revoked. (The Catholic Encyclopedia instead dates the declaration 16 November 1851; the discrepancy is recorded here, not resolved.)

stages.label: Rome — the 1846 apparition itself
stages.noDocument: No Roman doctrinal ruling on the apparition has been located, in either direction. The children's sealed secrets were carried to Pius IX in July 1851 and no published papal judgment on them or on the apparition followed; the 1910 Catholic Encyclopedia sums the position up as "As Rome uttered no decision the strife was prolonged between the disputants". The zero is not for want of Roman interest: in the autumn of 1852 Pius IX issued at least nine acts favouring the sanctuary, the confraternity, the missioners and the anniversary — they are the next rung — and the bishop who catalogued them in 1854, a sympathetic witness with every motive to claim more, wrote that "the Holy See has not formally pronounced upon the fact of La Salette. Her word, that final and decisive word, has not been uttered." The two Roman acts this chronology cites against the case, of 1915 and 1923, name Mélanie's secret texts and not the apparition; the 2016 act of the Congregation for Divine Worship inscribing the memorial of Our Lady of La Salette in the proper calendar for France concerns the liturgy and the devotion, not the truth of the 1846 event. Approval of this apparition rests where it was given in 1851: with the diocese.

stages.label: Rome — the cult, the pilgrimage and the missioners (not the apparition)
stages.who: Pius IX, by rescript, brief and indult
stages.outcome: Rome moved quickly, and on everything except the question. Within fifteen months of the diocesan judgment of September 1851, Pius IX made the sanctuary's high altar privileged in perpetuity (24 August 1852), let any visiting priest say a votive Mass of the Blessed Virgin there (26 August), granted five indulgences to the Confraternity of La Salette (26 August), a plenary indulgence to everyone who visits the church (3 September) and to those who follow the missioners' missions (3 September), gave the missioners faculties for blessing objects and the Scapular (7 September), erected the confraternity into an Archconfraternity of Our Lady of Reconciliation of La Salette (7 September), and permitted the whole diocese of Grenoble to solemnize 19 September each year (2 December). Every one of these acts presupposes the pilgrimage and none of them adjudicates it: they regulate worship, grant indulgences and empower a clergy. The rung is marked as an act on a related matter for that reason, and the source that lists the acts — Bishop Ullathorne, in 1854, writing to persuade — is also the source for the denial: "The Holy See has not formally pronounced upon the fact of La Salette." A reader who takes the speed and volume of these favours as Rome's verdict is making the inference the acts were careful not to make.

stages.label: Holy Office — Mélanie's "Secret de la Salette" (not the apparition)
stages.who: Supreme Sacred Congregation of the Holy Office
stages.outcome: The decree "Decretum circa vulgo dictum «Secret de la Salette»" (AAS 7 (1915), pp. 594–595) commands the faithful of every country not to treat or discuss the so-called Secret of La Salette in its various forms, or its application to present or future times, in books, pamphlets or articles, signed or anonymous, under pain of canonical sanctions. Its object is the secret texts. The same decree states expressly that it does not forbid devotion to the Blessed Virgin invoked as Reconciler of La Salette, and it leaves the diocesan judgment of 1851 on the apparition untouched.

stages.label: Holy Office — Mélanie's printed booklet (not the apparition)
stages.who: Supreme Sacred Congregation of the Holy Office; approved by Pius XI
stages.outcome: The Holy Office proscribed and condemned the booklet "L'apparition de la très Sainte Vierge sur la sainte montagne de la Salette" — the 1922 Société Saint-Augustin reprint of the text Mélanie published at Lecce in 1879 — ordering copies withdrawn from the hands of the faithful; Pius XI approved the resolution the same day (AAS 15 (1923), pp. 287–288). The condemned object is a printed book by one of the seers, not the apparition of 1846 and not the diocesan judgment of 1851.

events.title: Philibert de Bruillard is consecrated Bishop of Grenoble
events.text: Philibert de Bruillard, born at Dijon in 1765, ordained in 1789 and a clandestine priest through the Revolution, was consecrated Bishop of Grenoble by Bishop Frayssinous on 6 August 1826. Over his episcopate he established 107 new parishes and 34 vicariates and brought several congregations into the diocese, among them the Oblates of Mary Immaculate in 1834. He was therefore about eighty years old, and twenty years into rebuilding a post-Revolutionary diocese, when the two children of Corps made their report in September 1846. He resigned in 1852 and died on 15 December 1860; his heart is kept at the shrine. Recorded as the institutional setting of the judgment of 1851, not as a reason to accept or reject it.

events.dateNote: The crisis is dated to 1845–1847 as a whole; this entry is placed at 1846, the year of the failed harvest that preceded the reported apparition of 19 September.
events.title: The subsistence crisis of the Hungry Forties reaches its worst year
events.text: Potato blight arrived on the continent in the summer of 1845 and spread within weeks; the cereal harvests failed as well, and food prices reached their peak in the first half of 1847. France recorded roughly ten thousand famine-related deaths — far fewer than Ireland, and still a subsistence crisis of a kind Western Europe would not see again. Historians read the hardship as the main trigger of the political upheaval of 1848. In the Isère, per the French Wikipedia account, cereal production fell sharply and the price of bread doubled. The public message the children reported speaks of spoilt wheat and rotting potatoes; readers have drawn conclusions from that in both directions, and this dataset draws none. The crisis is recorded here as the material condition of the year, not as an explanation of the report and not as corroboration of it.

events.title: Two children report an apparition of a weeping "Beautiful Lady"
events.text: Mélanie Calvat (14) and Maximin Giraud (11), shepherd children from Corps, report that at about 3 p.m., on the mountain pasture above La Salette-Fallavaux, a weeping woman surrounded by light spoke to them — in French and then in the local Occitan dialect — delivering a public message centred on blasphemy, Sunday observance and conversion, and entrusting each child with a personal secret. All content of the event rests on the children's own accounts.

events.dateNote: The date is given by the French Wikipedia article, in the conditional mood it uses throughout for the reported events ("se seraient rendus", "auraient constaté"). No contemporary document establishing it was reachable from this session.
events.title: A spring is reported flowing at the apparition site
events.text: Two days after the reported apparition, inhabitants of La Salette are said to have gone up to the pasture and to have found clear water flowing abundantly at the spot where the children placed the weeping woman. The spring became the centre of the pilgrimage and of the cures later claimed there. The datable thing recorded here is the REPORT — who said what, and when it began to circulate. This dataset does not record that a spring appeared, nor that it had not been there before.

events.dateNote: The date is the one the French Wikipedia article gives for what it calls the first "declared miracle"; the underlying document was not reachable from this session.
events.title: The first cure is reported and circulated as a "declared miracle"
events.text: A woman who for twenty-two years had walked only on crutches, and had been bedridden for seven, is reported to have walked unaided after prayers were made for her at the site. It is the first of the claims that later brought the bishop to open a formal inquiry. The event dated here is the REPORTING, not a cure: this dataset does not record that anyone was healed. The French Wikipedia article notes of these "declarations of miracles" that the Church subjected them to no scientific inquiry — La Salette has no institution equivalent to the Lourdes Medical Bureau, and no cure connected with the shrine carries a separate act of recognition.

events.dateNote: The French Wikipedia article gives 19 July 1847 for the formal opening of the canonical inquiry and 13 December 1847 for the commission's vote. Both are recorded and both stay flagged: the source is tertiary, and the diocesan act itself was not reachable from this session. The sanctuary presents the 1851 judgment as the outcome of five years of inquiry; the Catholic Encyclopedia records only that Bishop de Bruillard appointed a commission, without dates.
events.title: Bishop de Bruillard opens the canonical investigation
events.text: Bishop Philibert de Bruillard of Grenoble orders an investigation of the children's report and appoints a commission of clergy and theologians to examine it judicially. What brought it to this point, on the French Wikipedia's account, was the reported cures and the press controversy around them, not the children's account alone: the commission interrogated the visionaries, the inhabitants and the local clergy, and also examined the cures being reported. The commission concludes, per the Catholic Encyclopedia, that the reality of the apparition should be admitted.

events.title: First anniversary: the congregation counts at least 30,000 on the mountain
events.text: The Missionaries' own timeline records "at least 30,000 pilgrims" going up the mountain on the first anniversary, and notes that by 1849 some 15,000 people had been inscribed in the Confraternity of Our Lady of La Salette, Reconciler. Both figures are the congregation's, published by the congregation, and are attributed to it here rather than asserted; no independent count for those years was reachable.

events.dateNote: Date from the French Wikipedia article; the commission's own minutes were not reachable from this session.
events.title: The episcopal commission votes in favour of the apparition
events.text: The commission of examiners appointed by Bishop de Bruillard votes, on the French Wikipedia's account, in favour of recognising the apparition — with a single dissenting voice. The vote is advice to the bishop, not a judgment: the diocesan judgment itself would not come for another four years, on 19 September 1851.

events.dateNote: The Google Books catalogue record gives 1848; the French Wikipedia article gives 1849. The disagreement is recorded rather than resolved — the title page could not be read directly, because the Gallica digitization returned 403 to this session's egress.
events.title: Canon Rousselot publishes his report to the bishop — the printed record of the reported cures
events.text: Pierre-Joseph Rousselot (1785–1865), professor of dogmatic theology at Grenoble, member of the commission and the leading advocate of the apparition's reality, published his report to the bishop as La vérité sur l'événement de La Salette du 19 septembre 1846. It is the document in which the cures claimed at the mountain entered the printed record, gathered and argued by a named ecclesiastic who believed them. That is what is dated here: a report about reported cures, by a partisan of the case, addressed to the authority that would judge it. What the cures were, this dataset does not say — the book itself was not readable from this session, and no cure recorded in it carries a Church act of its own.

events.dateNote: Maximin's text is dated Grenoble, 3 July 1851 and Mélanie's 6 July 1851 (Cor Jesu Sacratissimum, reprinting earlier accounts). Accounts differ on the carriers — canons Gerin and Rousselot in some accounts, vicars-general Melin and Rousselot in others — and the delivery to Pius IX is commonly dated 18 July 1851, a day not verified here against a reachable source.
events.title: The children's secrets are written down and sent to Pius IX
events.text: At the bishop's instance the two seers commit their personal secrets to paper — Maximin's letter is dated Grenoble, 3 July 1851, Mélanie's 6 July 1851 — and the sealed texts are carried to Rome by two envoys of Bishop de Bruillard and delivered to Pope Pius IX in July 1851. Accounts differ on the envoys' identity (canons Gerin and Rousselot, or vicars-general Melin and Rousselot). Neither text was published by the Holy See; Maximin's secret was never published at all.

events.dateNote: The doctrinal pronouncement is dated 19 September 1851 (sanctuary, Missionaries, Wikipedia). The 1910 Catholic Encyclopedia instead gives 16 November 1851 — read here as the date the mandement was published and read in the diocese's churches; the disagreement is recorded, not resolved.
events.title: Bishop de Bruillard declares the apparition worthy of belief
events.text: Five years to the day after the reported event, Bishop Philibert de Bruillard issues his doctrinal pronouncement: the apparition of the Blessed Virgin to the two shepherds on 19 September 1846 "bears within itself all the characteristics of truth", and the faithful are justified in believing it certain. This is the key diocesan approval document; the Catholic Encyclopedia dates the declaration 16 November 1851, a discrepancy recorded here rather than resolved.

events.dateNote: 1 May 1852 per the French and English Wikipedia articles; the congregation's own timeline speaks of a second doctrinal statement of the bishop dated 25 May — the day the cornerstone was laid. Both dates are carried.
events.title: Pastoral letter: a sanctuary decreed, the Missionaries of La Salette founded
events.text: Bishop de Bruillard publishes a pastoral letter announcing the construction of a sanctuary on the mountain of La Salette and creating a body of diocesan missionaries he names the Missionaries of Our Lady of La Salette, charged with serving the pilgrims and spreading the message the children reported.

events.title: Cornerstone of the sanctuary church laid on the mountain
events.text: The first stone of the church is laid on the apparition site at about 1,800 m altitude, before a large assembly of the faithful; the building was completed in 1865.

events.dateNote: The dates are Ullathorne's, published in 1854 and itemised act by act. The acts themselves predate the Holy See's printed gazettes — Acta Sanctae Sedis begins in 1865 — so none of them could be checked against an official text from this session.
events.title: Pius IX grants the new sanctuary a series of spiritual favours
events.text: In a fortnight, eleven months after the Bishop of Grenoble declared the apparition worthy of belief, Rome attaches a run of privileges to the site and to the works growing around it. Ullathorne, writing in 1854, lists them: a rescript of 24 August making the sanctuary's high altar a privileged altar in perpetuity; a rescript of 26 August allowing any priest who comes to La Salette to say a votive Mass of the Blessed Virgin on almost any day; a brief of the same day granting five indulgences to members of the Confraternity of La Salette; a brief of 3 September granting a plenary indulgence once a year to everyone who visits the church; a second brief of that date for those who follow the missioners' missions and retreats; and three briefs of 7 September — two giving the missioners the power to indulgence crosses, medals and beads and to give the Scapular, and one erecting the Confraternity into an Archconfraternity under the title of Our Lady of Reconciliation of La Salette. What these acts favour is the cult, the pilgrimage and the missioners. None of them pronounces on whether the apparition happened, and Ullathorne opens the chapter that lists them by saying so: "The Holy See has not formally pronounced upon the fact of La Salette. Her word, that final and decisive word, has not been uttered."

events.dateNote: Ullathorne's date, given as "2nd December" without the year restated; the year is his chapter's. The indult itself was not reached in its own text.
events.title: Indult: the anniversary of the apparition may be solemnized across the diocese
events.text: At the Bishop of Grenoble's request, Pius IX permits the 19th of September — the anniversary of the apparition, "vel ipso apparitionis die" — to be solemnized each year in all the churches of the diocese, or kept on the following Sunday with a solemn Mass and sung Vespers of the Blessed Virgin; the clergy may instead take the whole office and the Mass of the Patronage of the Blessed Virgin under solemn rite, as a Double of the Second Class. Ullathorne draws the inference his readers would draw and marks its limit in the same breath: the clergy "are not indeed enjoined, but they are permitted" to keep the day. A liturgical permission for one diocese is not a doctrinal judgment, and no doctrinal judgment followed it.

events.dateNote: Only the year is given by the source cited (the sanctuary's own history page); the date of Bishop Ginoulhiac's confirming statement was not verified against a reachable primary document.
events.title: Bishop Ginoulhiac confirms his predecessor's judgment
events.text: Jacques Ginoulhiac, de Bruillard's successor as Bishop of Grenoble, confirms the 1851 decision, stating — per the sanctuary's account — that "the task of the shepherds is complete; that of the Church begins."

events.title: The first Missionaries of La Salette take their vows
events.text: Fathers Albertin, Archier, Berlioz, Basson, Buisson and Petit took their first vows in the bishop's chapel, six years after the pastoral that created the body of diocesan missionaries. Their perpetual vows came in 1879, the same year Rome approved the Institute. Dates from the congregation's own timeline.

events.title: Death of Maximin Giraud
events.text: Maximin Giraud, who after unsettled years of study and odd employments had returned to his native Corps, dies there aged about 39. His personal secret was never published.

events.dateNote: Sources disagree on the day and even the month. The French Wikipedia articles give 20 August 1879 for the consecration and the crowning; the English article gives 21 August 1879 for the canonical coronation granted by Leo XIII; the congregation's own timeline places the crowning and consecration on 20–21 April 1879 and dates 18 August 1879 to the canonical approval of the Institute — a different act. The disagreement is recorded, not resolved: only the year is treated as verified.
events.title: The sanctuary church is consecrated and made a minor basilica
events.text: The church on the apparition site — begun in 1852 and finished after nearly three decades of building at 1,800 m — is officially consecrated and raised to the rank of minor basilica, and at the same ceremony the statue of Our Lady of La Salette receives a canonical coronation granted by Leo XIII. Cardinal Guibert, Archbishop of Paris, presided, according to the French Wikipedia account.

events.dateNote: The congregation's own timeline gives 18 August 1879 for the canonical approval of the Institute; the Roman decree itself was not reachable from this session.
events.title: Rome canonically approves the Missionaries of Our Lady of La Salette
events.text: The Institute founded by de Bruillard's pastoral of 1852 as a body of diocesan missionaries was canonically approved by Rome, per the congregation's own timeline, on 18 August 1879. This is a Roman act about a religious institute — its constitutions and its existence — and not a judgment on the apparition, which Rome has never ruled on. The two must not be read into one another.

events.title: Mélanie publishes her expanded secret at Lecce
events.text: Mélanie Calvat publishes at Lecce, as "L'apparition de la très Sainte Vierge sur la montagne de La Salette", a text of her secret far longer than the one sent to Pius IX in 1851, with the imprimatur of Salvatore Luigi Zola, Bishop of Lecce, who had received her in his diocese. The expanded text — including its much-quoted apocalyptic passages — is her own later redaction; its relation to what she wrote in 1851 is precisely what the subsequent controversy disputes.

events.dateNote: August 1880 per the Caterini letter as reported by the Wikipedia biography of Mélanie Calvat; the letter itself was not reachable and its exact date is not verified here.
events.title: The Holy Office asks that the Lecce booklet be withdrawn
events.text: After the Bishop of Troyes denounces the Lecce publication, Cardinal Prospero Caterini of the Holy Office writes — per the accounts cited — that the Holy Office is displeased with the book and wishes copies withdrawn from circulation. This is a disciplinary reaction to the expanded secret, not a revocation of the 1851 approval of the apparition.

events.title: The Missionaries spread beyond France
events.text: Fathers Pajot and Vignon reached Hartford, Connecticut in 1892, beginning the congregation's North American presence; earlier, from 1879, missionaries had served ten years in Norway. Madagascar followed in 1899, Poland in 1901–02 and Brazil in 1902, and by 1934 the congregation was organised in four provinces — France, Poland, Brazil and the United States. The English Wikipedia article states the Missionaries now serve in some twenty-five countries. Dates from the congregation's own timeline; the count of countries is attributed to Wikipedia and is not independently verified here.

events.dateNote: Sources disagree: 14 December 1904 (Wikipedia biography) versus 15 December 1904 (the 1910 Catholic Encyclopedia). She was found dead in the morning; the disagreement is recorded, not resolved.
events.title: Death of Mélanie Calvat
events.text: Mélanie Calvat dies at Altamura in southern Italy, where she had settled after decades of wandering between convents and countries. Sources disagree on the day — 14 December (Wikipedia) or 15 December (Catholic Encyclopedia).

events.dateNote: The French Wikipedia article dates the expulsion to the separation of Church and State (law of 9 December 1905) without giving a day for the shrine itself, and gives 1943 for the congregation's permanent return.
events.title: The congregation is expelled from the shrine under the separation laws
events.text: Under France's separation of Church and State the religious community was put out of the sanctuary and diocesan priests served it in their place. The Missionaries came back after the First World War and permanently in 1943. New roads in the 1960s made the mountain reachable for coach pilgrimages — and three coach crashes on the Laffrey descent, in 1973, 1975 and 2007, killed ninety-eight people between them.

events.title: Holy Office decree: the faithful ordered not to discuss the "Secret de la Salette"
events.text: The Supreme Sacred Congregation of the [[cdf-ddf|Holy Office]] issues a decree — "Decretum circa vulgo dictum «Secret de la Salette»" — commanding all the faithful, of every country, not to treat or discuss the so-called Secret of La Salette, its diverse forms, or its application to present or future times, under any pretext or form, in books, pamphlets or articles signed or anonymous, under pain of canonical sanctions. The decree states expressly that it does not forbid devotion to the Blessed Virgin invoked as Reconciler of La Salette. It disciplines discussion of the expanded secret; it does not touch the 1851 judgment on the apparition.

events.dateNote: The Holy Office's general session (Feria IV) condemned the booklet on 9 May 1923 and Pius XI approved the resolution the same day; the decree as printed in AAS 15 (1923), pp. 287–288, is dated from the Holy Office on 10 May 1923.
events.title: Mélanie's booklet is placed on the Index of Forbidden Books
events.text: The [[cdf-ddf|Holy Office]] proscribes and condemns the booklet "L'apparition de la très Sainte Vierge sur la sainte montagne de la Salette" — the 1922 Société Saint-Augustin reprint of the text published by Mélanie — ordering that copies be withdrawn from the hands of the faithful; Pope Pius XI approves the resolution. The condemnation names Mélanie's booklet, a separate object from the apparition approved in 1851.

events.title: The Association of the Pilgrims of Notre-Dame de La Salette is created
events.text: The sanctuary's own history page records the creation in 1962 of the Association des Pèlerins de Notre-Dame de La Salette, to maintain and administer the buildings and the infrastructure that a mountain shrine at 1,800 m requires. It is the civil body behind the pilgrimage as it now runs.

events.title: Our Lady of La Salette entered in the liturgical calendar for France
events.text: The Congregation for Divine Worship inscribes the celebration of Our Lady of La Salette in the proper liturgical calendar for France as an optional memorial on 19 September — a further act of the ordinary ecclesiastical recognition that has always concerned the apparition and the devotion, not the expanded secrets.

figures.name: Mélanie Calvat
figures.role: The elder of the two seers; a shepherd girl of Corps, aged 14 at the reported apparition (15 per the Catholic Encyclopedia). Later a religious in and out of several convents in France, England and Italy; author of the expanding versions of her secret culminating in the 1879 Lecce booklet.

figures.name: Maximin Giraud
figures.role: The younger seer; a shepherd boy of Corps, aged 11 at the reported apparition. His later life was unsettled — studies and employments taken up and abandoned — and his personal secret was never published. Died at Corps.

figures.name: Philibert de Bruillard
figures.role: Bishop of Grenoble at the time of the reported apparition. Ordered the canonical investigation, issued the doctrinal pronouncement of 19 September 1851 declaring the apparition worthy of belief, and by the pastoral of 1 May 1852 decreed the sanctuary and founded the Missionaries of Our Lady of La Salette.

figures.name: Jacques Ginoulhiac
figures.role: De Bruillard's successor as Bishop of Grenoble; confirmed the 1851 judgment in 1855, per the sanctuary's account.

figures.name: Salvatore Luigi Zola
figures.role: Bishop of Lecce; protector of Mélanie in her Italian years and grantor of the imprimatur for her 1879 booklet — the imprimatur of a local ordinary, not an approval by the Holy See.

organizations.name: Missionaries of Our Lady of La Salette
organizations.relation: Congregation of priests founded by Bishop de Bruillard's pastoral of 1 May 1852 to serve the sanctuary's pilgrims and spread the message the children reported; per the congregation's own timeline it was canonically approved by Rome on 18 August 1879. It is the shrine-serving institution, not a party to the secrets controversy.

organizations.name: Sanctuary of Our Lady of La Salette
organizations.relation: The shrine decreed by de Bruillard's 1852 pastoral on the apparition site; church begun 1852, completed 1865, consecrated and made a minor basilica in 1879. Its official history page is a preferred primary source for this dataset's institutional dates.

disambiguation.note: La Salette is contested terrain in a specific way: the same name covers an apparition approved by a bishop in 1851 and a body of later 'secret' texts restricted by the Holy Office in 1915 and 1923. Collapsing the two is the single most common error in the literature, sympathetic and critical alike.

items.title: Approved for pilgrimage is not the same as approved as an apparition — and that is the Church's rule, not this page's
items.text:
A shrine, a crowned image, a feast, indulgences, a papal visit: it is reasonable to read all that as the Church saying the apparition happened. It is not what the Church says it is doing, and since 2024 it says so in writing. The Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith's "Norms for Proceeding in the Discernment of Alleged Supernatural Phenomena" (17 May 2024) sets out six possible conclusions, and art. 23 makes the position explicit: "as a rule, neither the Diocesan Bishop, nor the Episcopal Conferences, nor the Dicastery will declare that these phenomena are of supernatural origin", though the Pope may authorise a special procedure. The ordinary favourable outcome is now "Nihil obstat", which art. 17 defines as acknowledging "many signs of the action of the Holy Spirit" in a spiritual experience "without expressing any certainty about the supernatural authenticity of the phenomenon itself". The document's own presentation adds that most shrines "have never had an official declaration of the supernatural nature of the events".

The reason is what a private revelation is. Public revelation closed with the apostles, so no apparition adds an article of faith, and even an approved one obliges no one to believe — the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith said exactly that when it published the third part of the Fátima secret in 2000. What a bishop is actually asked is a pastoral question: is this devotion safe, is it free of doctrinal error, is it bearing good fruit? That can be answered yes without answering the historical question, and usually is. The same acts are granted to devotions with no apparition behind them at all — Our Lady of the Rosary and Our Lady of Mount Carmel have feasts, crowned images and basilicas, and there is no reported apparition to approve.

So this page is not withholding approval; it is saying who gave which one, about what. Where a bishop did rule on an apparition, the ladder says so in his own words and marks the rung favourable — Lourdes 1862 and La Salette 1851 are quoted verbatim, Fátima 1930 is cited to its pastoral letter. What the ladder refuses to do is upgrade a crown into a verdict. If it did, a case a bishop examined and endorsed would look identical to a case nobody ever ruled on, because both have pilgrims; and the reverse error would follow just as easily, reading a Roman act against one seer's later writings as Rome condemning the apparition. Keeping the objects apart is the only way the chart carries information at all. Where the sources themselves say the Church's recognition is "implicit", the page records that word too, and does not promote it.

items.title: The apparition ≠ the "Secret of La Salette"
items.text: The 1851 approval and the later disciplinary acts are separate judgments about separate objects. Bishop de Bruillard's 19 September 1851 pronouncement declared the apparition itself worthy of belief. The Holy Office's 1915 decree and the 1923 Index placement concern Mélanie's later, expanded secret texts — the 1915 decree even states expressly that devotion to Our Lady of La Salette is not forbidden. Neither act revokes the other.

items.title: "Pius IX approved La Salette on 19 September 1851" — the date is the bishop's
items.text: A version of the story in wide circulation has Pius IX formally approving the public devotion and the prayers to Our Lady of La Salette on 19 September 1851. The date is real and the author is not. 19 September 1851 is the day Philibert de Bruillard, Bishop of Grenoble, issued the doctrinal pronouncement that judged the apparition to bear "all the characteristics of truth" and authorised the cult — an episcopal act, in a diocese, at the close of a four-year commission, and the act on which the approval of La Salette rests to this day. Pius IX had read the children's sealed secrets that July and issued nothing on them. What he did issue came eleven months later and is recorded on this page: nine acts between 24 August and 2 December 1852, favouring the sanctuary, the confraternity, the missioners and the anniversary, catalogued by Bishop Ullathorne in 1854 — who opens the same chapter by writing that "the Holy See has not formally pronounced upon the fact of La Salette". So the claim is right that the devotion and the prayers were papally favoured, wrong about the year, and wrong about whose act 19 September 1851 was. The confusion runs the same way at Lourdes, where a "decree of approval by Pius IX of 1 February 1876" turns out to be the decree of canonical coronation: a real papal document, relabelled in retelling as approval of an apparition no pope has ruled on.

items.title: Reported, not asserted
items.text: Everything said about the 19 September 1846 event rests on the accounts of two children, examined and judged credible by a diocesan investigation. This dataset records who reported what and when, and what the Church ruled and when; it does not assert the supernatural claim as fact, and it does not deny it either.

items.title: The 1851 secret ≠ the 1879 text
items.text: What Mélanie wrote for Pius IX in July 1851 and what she published at Lecce in 1879 are not established to be the same text: the 1879 booklet is far longer, and her versions grew over the intervening decades. Which text is 'the' secret is exactly what the controversy disputes; this dataset carries the dispute, attributed and dated, without resolving it.

items.title: La Salette-Fallavaux ≠ the sanctuary
items.text: La Salette-Fallavaux is the Alpine commune; the reported apparition site and the basilica stand on the mountain above it, at about 1,800 m. "La Salette" also names the two religious congregations born of the shrine (the Missionaries and the Sisters), which are institutions, not the event.

items.title: A reported cure ≠ a recognized miracle
items.text: The cures claimed at La Salette are part of this record in exactly one way: as REPORTS. The event dated is the reporting — who claimed a cure, when the claim began to circulate, and when the commission or Canon Rousselot's printed report took it up. No cure is recorded as having happened, and no beneficiary is named in a title. Nor is there a recognition act to record: unlike Lourdes, La Salette has no medical bureau and no bishop's declaration that a named cure is miraculous. The cures were part of the evidence the diocesan judgment of 1851 weighed; they are not themselves approved miracles, and the 1851 judgment is about the apparition, not about them.

references.publisher: William Bernard Ullathorne, Bishop of Birmingham / Internet Archive scan
references.publisherNote: Near-contemporary devotional account by an English bishop who visited La Salette in 1854 and interviewed both seers; sympathetic to the apparition and explicit about it. Cited here for its chapter XI, which enumerates nine Roman acts of 1852 by their kind and date, and which opens by stating that the Holy See had not pronounced on the fact of the apparition — a denial from a witness whose interest ran the other way. The individual rescripts, briefs and the indult have not been read here in their own text: they predate both Acta Sanctae Sedis (1865) and Acta Apostolicae Sedis (1909), so the Holy See's online act archives cannot contain them, and no other transcription was reached from this session. The full text was read from the Internet Archive scan (Google-digitized copy, holymountainlas00ullagoog).
